title: Courted by Both Parties, Indian-American Voters Head Into Midterms Leaning Democratic — and Independent
excerpt: A summer AAPI survey puts Democratic House candidates ahead 66% to 18% among Indian-American voters, while Carnegie's data shows independents climbing to 29% — the bloc both parties are now fighting over.
body:
• The 2026 Asian American Voter Survey found 92% of Indian-American registered voters plan to vote in the November 3 midterms — the highest enthusiasm increase of any major Asian ethnic group surveyed.
  • Democratic candidates lead among Indian-American voters by 66% to 18% in House races and 66% to 22% in Senate races, and 74% view President Trump unfavourably.
  • Carnegie's 2026 Indian American Attitudes Survey shows the deeper shift: Democratic identification has fallen from 52% in 2020 to 46%, Republican identification has risen to 19%, and independents now make up 29%.
  • Cost of living and inflation — cited as very or extremely important by 90% of Asian-American voters — outweigh India-specific issues such as H-1B policy and tariffs for most voters.

Three weeks before the November 3 midterms, both parties are courting a community of about 5.5 million people with a message tailored to it — and the survey data explains why neither side can take Indian-American voters for granted. The community leans Democratic by wide margins, votes at high rates, and is quietly becoming less attached to either party, according to the 2026 Asian American Voter Survey reported by IANS.

The numbers both campaigns are reading

Enthusiasm is the headline figure. Ninety-two per cent of Indian-American registered voters said they planned to vote, 74% were absolutely certain they would cast a ballot, and 43% said they were more enthusiastic than usual — the largest increase in enthusiasm among the major Asian ethnic groups in the survey. On preference, Democratic Senate candidates led Republicans 66% to 22% among Indian-American voters, and Democratic House candidates led 66% to 18%. Three-quarters of respondents viewed President Donald Trump unfavourably, including 56% who held a very unfavourable opinion.

But the trend underneath the topline is what strategists are watching. Carnegie's 2026 Indian American Attitudes Survey found Democratic identification down to 46% from 52% in 2020, Republican identification up to 19% from 15%, and — most strikingly — independents at 29%, up from 23% in 2020. In 2024, Carnegie measured 61% of Indian-American registered voters intending to vote for Kamala Harris against 31% for Trump, already a marked shift from 2020's 72% to 22%. The community is not flipping; it is loosening.

Why the wooing looks different this cycle

Republicans are fielding visible Indian-American candidates even where the terrain is hostile — at least nine are on the November ballot, including Vivek Ramaswamy in Ohio's toss-up governor's race — while running into the party's own hardening line on H-1B visas, the route by which many Indian-American families arrived. Democrats, meanwhile, have watched three Indian-American incumbents and candidates fall to left-wing primary challengers this cycle, and the informal "Samosa Caucus" in the House is set to shrink as two members exit. Both parties are thus selling to the community while their own Indian-American benches change shape.

What will actually decide these votes

The survey evidence points away from diaspora-specific issues as the deciding factor. Cost of living and inflation dominate — rated very or extremely important by 90% of Asian-American voters — followed by healthcare, jobs, Social Security and education. H-1B restrictions and US-India tariff friction anger many Indian-American voters, but the data suggests a voter can oppose both and still vote on taxes and grocery prices. For campaigns, that means the pitch that lands in Edison, Fremont and Sugar Land looks much like the pitch everywhere else — with the community's 29% independent share making it worth making carefully.
